content: Ammonium bicarbonate, also known as bicarbonate of ammonia, ammonium hydrogen carbonate, hartshorn, or powdered baking ammonia, is the bicarbonate salt of ammonia. It is produced by passing carbon dioxide through a solution of ammonia, resulting in the formation of a white, odorless powder that is only slightly soluble in water. When exposed to air or heat, its aqueous solution releases carbon dioxide and becomes alkaline. Upon boiling, aqueous solutions of ammonium bicarbonate decompose, releasing carbon dioxide and ammonia. At room temperature, ammonium bicarbonate appears as a white crystalline powder with a faint ammonia-like odor. It dissolves in water to form a mildly alkaline solution but is insoluble in acetone and alcohols. When heated to temperatures between 36°C and 60°C, it decomposes into ammonia, carbon dioxide, and water vapor in an endothermic reaction, which causes a cooling effect. When it reacts with acids, carbon dioxide is released, while reactions with alkalis produce ammonia. Historically, ammonium bicarbonate was used in the food industry as a leavening agent, particularly in recipes like gingerbread or Chinese youtiao, before the widespread adoption of baking soda. It is still used in some food products and is often referred to as hartshorn or hornsalt in Scandinavian baking recipes, though it can be substituted with baking soda. In agriculture, it has been used as a nitrogen fertilizer, especially in China, but is gradually being replaced by urea due to its lower quality and instability. Beyond food and agriculture, ammonium bicarbonate is utilized in the production of fire-extinguishing compounds, pharmaceuticals, dyes, pigments, and as a source of ammonia in basic fertilizers. It also finds applications in the plastic and rubber industries, ceramic manufacturing, chrome leather tanning, and the synthesis of catalysts. From a safety perspective, ammonium bicarbonate is an irritant to the skin, eyes, and respiratory system. Additionally, during baking, it can contribute to the formation of acrylamide, a compound linked to cancer in laboratory animals.
